evals.prompt: Define the client-server boundary in a unified codebase in 2-3 sentences. Name the three governing properties.
expected_elements: The line at which execution context changes between a server runtime (filesystem, secrets, DB) and a client runtime (browser sandbox, no secrets)
Anything crossing must be serialized — encoded as bytes on one side, decoded on the other
Names the three properties: serialization, direction, trust
Notes directives make the boundary syntactically visible but do not create it

evals.prompt: Why does the same TypeScript type appearing on both sides of the boundary not make the boundary go away?
expected_elements: Types are a compile-time claim; the runtime boundary is a serialization-and-trust event regardless
Values lose their type when they cross — the type system stops at the boundary until parsed on the other side
A Date becomes a string in JSON; a function becomes an opaque RSC token, not a real function
Client→server input is adversarial no matter what type it is annotated as

evals.prompt: What does explicitly marking the boundary with directives cost, and what does it buy? Why is the ceremony worth it?
expected_elements: Cost: a small upfront ceremony ('use client'/'use server'/'server-only'/'client-only' markers)
Benefit: legibility and refactor safety — the boundary becomes visible and the bundler can catch leaks
Without explicit marking, a unified codebase silently leaks secrets, ships server modules, and trusts adversaries
Frames the directives as marks that make an always-present boundary visible

evals.prompt: A teammate wants to pass a server-built Map<string, User> and an onClick callback as props to a 'use client' component. Walk through what survives the boundary and what must change.
expected_elements: A Map does not cross plain JSON (only structured clone / RSC can); convert to an array of [key, value] pairs for JSON
A closure/callback cannot cross — only data, server-action references, and RSC primitives can
Use a 'use server' function (serializes as an RPC reference) or pass the data and reconstruct behavior client-side
States the practical rule: if you cannot describe the value in bytes, it cannot cross

evals.prompt: Write the correct discipline for a server action updateUserName(rawInput). What four steps must it perform and why?
expected_elements: Authenticate the caller from a server-authoritative source (session), not the client's claim
Validate rawInput with a runtime schema — TypeScript types are not validation; bytes from the client may be anything
Authorize the action — the authenticated user may not be allowed to operate on input.userId
Perform the action only after the above; treats the action as an RPC handler with a hostile caller

evals.prompt: Distinguish client-server-boundary from rendering-models, http-semantics, api-design, and type-safety by the mechanism each owns.
expected_elements: rendering-models owns staging of work across build/request/stream/interaction; this skill owns the serialization frontier — they compose
http-semantics owns the wire protocol (verbs, status, headers, caching); this skill is upstream, deciding what data exists at the boundary and how it is encoded
api-design owns the external API surface; this skill owns the in-program server/client boundary inside one unified codebase
type-safety owns compile-time checking; this skill is where the type system stops at runtime

evals.prompt: A developer says a server action 'is just a normal async function I import and call.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: A server action looks like a local call (await sendEmail(formData)) but is an HTTP POST / RPC handler
The caller on the other side of the network is hostile — every byte is adversarial
It must parse, validate, authenticate, authorize, and rate-limit; a local-call mental model skips all of that
The 'use server' directive marks the function as network-reachable, not as a local helper

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a codebase handles the client-server boundary correctly?
expected_elements: Client-shipped files carry 'use client'; server actions carry 'use server' — the implicit-server default is intentional
Server actions validate input with a runtime schema and re-derive trust from a server-authoritative source
Secret-holding modules import 'server-only'; browser-global modules import 'client-only' — the bundler errors on leaks
Props from server to client are serializable in the project's wire format; no closures cross
Auth, authorization, and rate-limiting live in server actions/route handlers, not client components
